So, seven days. How many are you giving Tokyo, and how many Kyoto?
Four and three, I think. My dad wants a great deal of time in Tokyo for the museums.
That works. Tokyo is bustling, and you will find plenty of nightlife there: arcades, karaoke, all of it.
And Kyoto? People say it is more low-key.
Much more. There is hardly any nightlife, but the scenery is incredible, and a few of the best temples are free.
I saw photos of the bamboo forest. It looks amazing.
It is, if you go off-peak. After nine it is completely overcrowded, and you will get very little out of it.
So Tokyo or Kyoto, if you had to choose only one?
Neither! Keep both, and use one day for a day trip to Nara. Few people regret that.

Hi Mark. Last class the trip went wrong, and you explained why. Today the trip goes right, and you have to decide where to spend it. To compare two places well, you need to say how much of everything each one has, and a lot of and not many are too vague for that. Start with hardly any. It means almost none, and it is already negative, so you say hardly any tourists, never hardly no tourists. Then a great deal of, for things you cannot count, like time, history or noise. Kyoto has a great deal of history. For things you can count, like temples or trains, say a great many, or a large number of. Now the most important pair. Few, without a, is small and disappointing. Few people speak English there, so it can be hard. A few, with a, is small and good. A few of the temples were free, so we saved money. It is the same number, and the opposite feeling. Little and a little work the same way, but only with things you cannot count, like time or money. Plenty of means more than enough. Fewer is for things you count, and less is for things you do not. Fewer tourists, less noise. And when there are exactly two cities, use both, neither and either. Neither city was cheap, but both were worth it. Before class, compare two places you know, and use at least five of these.

Hello, this is Daisuke from Kyoto Walks. Thank you for your email. You asked whether your family should stay in Kyoto or in Osaka, so here is my honest answer. Both cities are wonderful, and neither is a bad choice, but they are very different. Kyoto has a great deal of history. There are a large number of temples and shrines, and a few of them are free. The problem is the crowds. The most famous places are overcrowded after ten in the morning, so go early, when there are hardly any tourists. At night, though, Kyoto is quiet. There is very little nightlife, and most restaurants close at nine. Osaka is the opposite. It has fewer temples and less history to see, but plenty of food, plenty of noise and plenty of things to do after dark. If you are traveling with a teenager, that matters. My suggestion is simple. Sleep in Osaka, and take a day trip to Kyoto. The train takes less than thirty minutes, and either station is easy to find. Few families regret that plan. Write to me if you have any questions, and enjoy your trip.

On the first two days, walk around Tokyo to get a feel for the city, because it is so bustling that you need time to adjust. On day three, visit the famous landmarks early, when there are hardly any tourists. On day four, take the fast train to Kyoto, which has a great deal of history and far less noise. On day five, see a few of the temples off-peak, before the crowds arrive. On the last day, take a day trip to Nara, which few visitors regret.
